title: Two Sum
problem_statement: Given a list of integers and a target, determine whether two elements at different indices add up to the target. Each list element may be used only once in a pair; two equal values can form a valid pair only if they occur at two separate indices. Print `YES` if a valid pair exists and `NO` otherwise. Aim for expected O(n) time using a set while scanning the list.
input_format: Three lines. The first line contains n, the number of values. The second line contains exactly n space-separated integers; if n is 0, this line is blank. The third line contains the target integer.
output_format: Print exactly `YES` if two values from different indices sum to the target; otherwise print exactly `NO`.
starter_code:
def main():
    n = int(input())
    values_line = input()
    numbers = list(map(int, values_line.split()))
    target = int(input())

    # TODO: Keep track of values from earlier indices as you scan.
    # TODO: Check whether a needed partner has already appeared.
    print("NO")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

public_samples.explanation: The values 2 and 7 are at different indices and add to 9.
The two 3 values occur at distinct indices and add to 6.
The single 3 cannot be used twice; only one list index is available.
No two distinct list elements add to 8.
An empty list contains no pair, even when the target is zero.
-1 and 8 occur at different indices and add to 7.

hints: For each value, ask what partner would be needed to reach the target.
Remember that a partner must come from a different index. Previously seen values are safe candidates; the current value should not be paired with itself before it has been recorded.
Scan once while storing prior values in a set. For each number, check whether `target - number` is already in the set, then add the current number if no pair was found. This gives expected O(n) time.
common_beginner_mistakes: Using the current number as its own partner when only one matching element exists.
Checking for a complement after adding the current number to the seen set, which can incorrectly reuse the same index.
Checking whether the target itself is in the list instead of checking for two addends.
Forgetting that duplicate values at different indices can form a valid pair.
Returning `YES` as soon as any number is seen without confirming its complement.
Using nested loops over every pair, which can take O(n squared) time for large lists.
Failing to handle n = 0 and its required blank values line.
completion_criteria: Reads exactly three lines, including a blank second line when n is 0.
Uses two distinct indices for every candidate pair.
Correctly handles repeated values, negative values, and empty or one-element lists.
Uses a set-based scan with expected O(n) time.
Prints exactly `YES` or `NO` with no additional output.
Passes all public samples and separately maintained private tests.
